article.overview: A radio interferometer is a set of separated radio antennas whose signals are combined (correlated) so that the group behaves like a single, larger telescope. On the Moon, the main reason for building one is the far side, which always faces away from Earth and is shielded from human-made radio interference and from the ionosphere that limits low-frequency radio astronomy from the ground. The sources reviewed show that lunar radio interferometry is still largely at the concept and early-demonstration stage. Several small lunar radio experiments have flown or are planned, but no full-scale lunar radio interferometer has been deployed.
article.description: A radio interferometer measures the same radio waves at several points and compares them. Each antenna records a time-stamped voltage. When these recordings are cross-correlated, the result depends on the direction of the sky and on the spacing between the antennas, known as the baseline. Longer baselines give finer angular detail, which is why a few antennas spread over several kilometres can resolve structures that a single antenna cannot. Low-frequency lunar radio interferometers would normally use simple dipole or monopole antennas, a receiver that digitises the signal, and an onboard or downlinked spectrometer or correlator, together with a power and communications system because the far side has no direct line of sight to Earth. The term describes the scientific technique rather than one standard hardware design. The examples discussed differ considerably: some are single-spacecraft or single-lander instruments that measure radio spectra, while others are proposed multi-antenna arrays. Only some are true interferometers in the strict sense.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The sources reviewed describe several goals for low-frequency lunar radio instruments. These include imaging the low-frequency radio sky, including the Milky Way and the Sun, with the far side's radio quiet as the main advantage [1]; measuring the cosmic Dark Ages 21 cm hydrogen signal at redshifts of about z = 50 to 100, with calibration from an orbiting beacon, as named in the FARSIDE study [1]; monitoring solar and stellar radio bursts that can be linked to coronal mass ejections and energetic particle events [1]; studying the electron density of the plasma about 1 to 3 m above the surface, which affects how antennas on the Moon respond to signals [4]; measuring the low-frequency galactic background spectrum, where the ROLSES-1 team reported constraints from five minutes of raw waveforms [3]; investigating ionospheric effects on terrestrial shortwave transmissions, which ROLSES-1 detected and which the authors describe as terrestrial technosignatures [3]; and sounding the lunar subsurface, a secondary goal listed in the FARSIDE study [1]. Most of these goals are stated as design objectives or projections. Only the ROLSES-1 observations and the Longjiang-2 commissioning results are reported as measured outcomes in the sources read.
article.operating_principle: Two or more antennas receive the same radio wave at slightly different times, because the path length to each antenna differs. The time difference depends on the direction of the source and the spacing between antennas, and combining the signals reveals this directional information. A radio wavelength is the speed of light divided by the frequency: about 10 m at 30 MHz and about 300 m at 1 MHz. For a given baseline, finer angular detail can be resolved at higher frequency. In a lunar instrument, each antenna output is amplified, filtered, digitised and processed. The generic chain is as follows. A dipole or monopole antenna picks up a wide band of frequencies. A receiver amplifies and digitises the voltage; the ROLSES-1 electronics were described as sampling at 14 bits and 120 million samples per second [4]. An FPGA or similar digital processor performs a Fourier transform to create spectra, and cross-correlation between antennas produces interferometric information [3][4][5]. Data are stored onboard and telemetered to Earth through a relay or lander link, and raw waveforms are sometimes downlinked for later analysis; the ROLSES-1 team states that raw waveform telemetry is useful for studying dust impacts on the antennas [4]. The far side is shielded from Earth's ionosphere, which blocks radio waves below roughly 10 to 15 MHz; the ROLSES-1 paper gives about 15 MHz for this cutoff [4].
article.scientific_importance: Radio observations below about 30 MHz are one of the least explored parts of the electromagnetic spectrum from space. The lunar far side is considered a suitable place for this work because it is free of Earth-generated interference and of the ionosphere. The evidence base is still small. The FARSIDE study is a design proposal [1]; the Longjiang-2 mission produced in-orbit commissioning results [2]; and ROLSES-1 produced early measurements from a short surface operation [3]. LuSEE-Night was planned but, according to the sources read, had not launched at the time of the most recent search [5][6].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size, frequency range or power budget for a radio interferometer. The sources reviewed describe very different designs, from a microsatellite in lunar orbit to a proposed 128-antenna array. The values below describe specific named examples only and should not be treated as typical values for the payload class. Where a value was not found in the sources read, the entry says so.

examples.name: Longjiang-2 Low-Frequency Interferometer and Spectrometer (LFIS)
examples.type: Flown lunar-orbit instrument (in-orbit commissioning and first results reported)
examples.platform: Longjiang-2 microsatellite in a selenocentric (lunar) orbit. A secondary summary says it flew with the Queqiao relay satellite [2][7].
examples.frequency_range_status: Not stated in the abstract read [2]. A secondary summary gives 1 to 30 MHz; not verified against the full paper.
examples.channels_status: Not stated in the abstract read. A secondary summary gives three channels; not verified.
examples.spectral_resolution_status: Not stated in the abstract read. A secondary summary gives better than 0.1 MHz; not verified.
examples.time_synchronization_status: Not stated in the abstract read. A secondary summary gives about 3.3 ns; not verified.
examples.operating_mode: The abstract does not confirm whether interferometric operation was achieved. A secondary summary states that the experiment ran in single-telescope mode with Longjiang-2 alone, because Longjiang-1 did not reach lunar orbit [2][7]. Not confirmed by the abstract read.
examples.measured_results: In-orbit commissioning confirmed reliable operation of the instrument. The RFI level below a few MHz was found to be below the receiver noise floor [2]. An RFI suppression of about 80 dB is given as an estimate of what is needed at lunar distance; it is an estimate, not a measurement [2].
examples.operational_duration: A secondary summary describes about one year in lunar orbit, followed by a deliberate deorbit onto the surface in July 2019. Not verified against the full paper [7].

examples.name: FARSIDE (proposed, notional architecture)
examples.type: Proposed NASA probe-class concept; design study, not a flown or funded mission [1]
examples.array_extent_status: Spread across an area of about 10 km [1]. A secondary summary gives four petals of 32 nodes; not verified against the full study [8].
examples.deployment: A rover deploys the antennas, which remain tethered to a central base station [1].
examples.power_and_communications: The base station provides central processing, power and data transmission to the Lunar Gateway. The power source is not specified in the abstract read [1].
examples.requirements_status: The study says the architecture is broadly consistent with the requirements for a Probe mission. This describes requirement alignment, not demonstrated performance [1].
examples.precursor_note: A secondary summary describes a six-antenna-node precursor called PRIME. Not verified against a primary source in this run [8].

examples.name: ROLSES-1 (Radio-wave Observations at the Lunar Surface of the photoElectron Sheath)
examples.type: Flown lunar-surface radio instrument on the Intuitive Machines-1 (Odysseus) lander; described by NASA-linked authors as NASA's first radio telescope on the Moon [3][4]
examples.antenna_type: 2.5 m radio monopoles, stowed during launch and deployed after landing with a frangibolt mechanism [4]
examples.frequency_range_status: 2 kHz to 30 MHz per the 2026 paper, with the low end below the ionospheric cutoff [4]. An earlier 2021 NASA-linked paper gave 10 kHz to 30 MHz [9]; the more recent paper is used here.
examples.electronics: Digitised at 14 bits and 120 million samples per second, then processed by an FPGA that runs a Fourier transform. Time-averaged spectra are stored and raw waveforms are telemetered [4].
examples.measured_results: All four antennas recorded shortwave transmissions from Earth that penetrated the ionosphere, which the authors describe as terrestrial technosignatures. The authors constrained the amplitude of the low-frequency isotropic galactic spectrum using five minutes of raw waveforms from the least noisy antenna [3].
examples.operational_duration: A small amount of data was collected over fractions of one day during cruise and about two days on the lunar surface [3]. The 2026 paper does not give a surface duration in the abstract read [4].
examples.landing_note: Described as a tilted landing near the lunar south pole. The abstract does not give the tilt angle or its effect on power or data [4].

examples.name: LuSEE-Night (Lunar Surface Electromagnetics Experiment)
examples.type: Planned NASA-sponsored lunar farside radio instrument on Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 2; not launched in the most recent sources found [5][6]
examples.antenna_type: Two orthogonal electric dipoles, each about 6 m tip-to-tip, according to the design paper [5]
examples.antenna_conflict_note: A search summary describes four monopoles about 3 m long on a motor-driven carousel [10]. This conflicts with the design paper; the design paper is used here.
examples.receiver: Four-channel baseband receiver with a 50 MHz Nyquist rate, according to the design paper [5]. Conventional frequency coverage of such a system is roughly 0 to 25 MHz; this is an inference, not a stated value.
examples.power_and_survival: Intended to operate standalone through the lunar night, which lasts about 14 Earth days [5][10]. A search summary cites a battery of about 40 kg [10]; not verified against the full paper.
examples.measured_values: None. The design paper reports only design and planned values [5].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The examples use different scales and architectures. Longjiang-2 is a microsatellite in lunar orbit, ROLSES-1 has four 2.5 m monopoles on a surface lander, LuSEE-Night has dipoles about 6 m tip-to-tip on a lander top deck, and the FARSIDE concept spreads 128 antennas over about 10 km. These dimensions are not directly comparable. A new instrument would need its dimensions set by its intended frequency range, baseline and sensitivity.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass values are not publicly specified for most examples in the sources read. The Longjiang-2 abstract read does not give its mass; the ROLSES-1 and FARSIDE abstracts do not give mass; the LuSEE-Night design paper does not give mass in the summary read. A secondary summary cites a LuSEE-Night battery of about 40 kg, which is not verified [10].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified for the examples read, apart from the secondary summary of the LuSEE-Night battery [10] and the FARSIDE base-station architecture, whose power source is not specified [1].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Lunar radio instruments operate in an environment with extreme temperature swings, no atmosphere, radiation exposure and dust. The ROLSES-1 team states that raw waveform telemetry is useful for studying dust impacts on antennas [4]. The far side is radio-quiet, which is valuable for science, but a lander or relay still needs power and communications. Lunar night is a major operational constraint. LuSEE-Night is intended to operate through the night, which lasts about 14 Earth days [5][10]. A secondary source says the Blue Ghost lander will power down before lunar night so that it does not interfere with the radio instrument [6]. For a multi-antenna array, precise knowledge of antenna positions matters, and errors in position or timing reduce the quality of the interferometric result. The Longjiang-2 abstract read does not give its timing performance [2]. Any future array would need a reliable clock and a method to determine its own geometry on the surface.
article.limitations: Not every example is an interferometer. ROLSES-1 and LuSEE-Night are primarily radio spectrometers on a single platform, and the sources read do not establish interferometric operation for either [3][5]. Longjiang-2 may have operated in single-telescope mode; the abstract read does not confirm whether interferometry was achieved [2]. Earth's ionosphere limits ground-based observations below about 10 to 15 MHz, so far-side measurements depend on the spacecraft or relay that carries the instrument [4]. Measurements are affected by the instrument's own electronics, the lander or spacecraft's electromagnetic environment and surface dust and temperature changes. The LuSEE-Night design aims to avoid lander electromagnetic interference, but the sources read do not show how well this was achieved [5]. Several numbers vary between sources; the LuSEE-Night antenna geometry and the ROLSES-1 frequency range are examples, and this article uses the primary paper where one was available.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Lunar radio interferometers would be delivered as part of a lander, relay or dedicated spacecraft. Typical steps are integration on Earth, launch, lunar transfer, landing or orbit insertion, deployment and commissioning. The examples read show four different transport models: a lunar-orbit microsatellite, a surface lander payload, a proposed rover-deployed array, and a lander-integrated planned payload.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument with its spacecraft, relay or lander on Earth.
Launch the spacecraft using a launch vehicle.
Transfer to the Moon, or enter lunar orbit (Longjiang-2 case).
Land the payload on the lunar surface, or deliver it into orbit.
Deploy antennas (stowed for launch, deployed after landing in the ROLSES-1 case; deployed by a rover in the FARSIDE concept).
Commission the instrument and connect its power, data and relay interfaces.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Longjiang-2 flew as a microsatellite in a selenocentric orbit; a secondary summary links it to the Queqiao relay mission [7]. ROLSES-1 was installed on the Odysseus lander, with its four monopole antennas stowed for launch and deployed after landing with a frangibolt mechanism [4]. The FARSIDE concept uses a rover to deploy antennas tethered to a base station, with the base station relaying data to the Lunar Gateway [1]. LuSEE-Night is planned to sit on the top deck of the Blue Ghost Mission 2 lander and operate after landing on the lunar far side; the lander is planned to power down before lunar night [5][6].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Longjiang-2 was an in-orbit low-frequency experiment [2]. ROLSES-1 was a surface instrument on the Odysseus lander, described as NASA's first radio telescope on the Moon [3][4]. ROLSES-2 and LuSEE-Night are described as later successors [3][5].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with any specific lander or spacecraft has not been verified. The examples describe mission-level integration only, not a general interface specification. LuSEE-Night's planned carriage on Blue Ghost Mission 2 is a stated plan [5][6], but the launch date is unsettled in the sources read.

article.historical_significance: The Longjiang-2 paper is titled as the first results of a low-frequency experiment from a selenocentric orbit [2]. The ROLSES-1 results paper is titled as NASA's first radio telescope on the Moon and reports measured observations of terrestrial shortwave transmissions and the low-frequency galactic background [3]. LuSEE-Night and ROLSES-2 are described as successors that would extend this work later in the decade [3][5]. The FARSIDE study remains a design study and is cited here as a reference architecture for future far-side arrays [1].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The article draws on the arXiv abstract pages for most sources. Full-text PDFs were not read in this run, so numerical values that appear only in full text may be missing or incorrect. The Longjiang-2 frequency range, channel count, time synchronization and operating mode are not verified against the primary paper [2]. The FARSIDE layout, power architecture and sensitivity are not verified against the full study [1]. ROLSES-1 mass, power and surface operations duration are not verified [3][4]. LuSEE-Night antenna geometry, power system and launch schedule are unresolved; the design paper and the search summaries disagree on the antenna form [5][10]. The current status of Blue Ghost Mission 2 and LuSEE-Night was not confirmed; the sources read give a launch target in 2027, with date status TBD [6]. Lunar location recommendations are not included, as the user deferred them.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image URLs were verified in this run, so no image objects are included. Section-level image arrays are present but empty.

data_quality_notes: Only arXiv abstract pages and secondary search summaries were read for most sources. Full-text PDFs were not read in this run.
No image was verified from an official page or direct asset URL, so no images are included in the registry or section arrays.
Longjiang-2 frequency range, channel count, spectral resolution, time synchronization and operating mode come from a secondary summary and are not confirmed against the primary paper.
LuSEE-Night antenna geometry conflicts between the design paper (two 6 m dipoles) and a secondary summary (four 3 m monopoles); the design paper is used.
ROLSES-1 frequency range differs between a 2021 paper (10 kHz to 30 MHz) and the 2026 paper (2 kHz to 30 MHz); the 2026 paper is used.
ROLSES-1 landing is described as tilted in the 2026 abstract; a secondary summary described a tip-over. Extent and effect on power and data are not verified.
LuSEE-Night launch status is unsettled; the most recent sources found list the launch as TBD, with a 2027 target.

Catalogue entry 237 is a class of instrument, not a single design. Not all examples are strictly interferometers; ROLSES-1 and LuSEE-Night are primarily radio spectrometers on single platforms in the sources read.
